title: Cosmic fairy lights
caption: The globular cluster Messier 5, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: Messier 5 · constellation Serpens Caput · about 25000 light-years away (source figure)

recognition.text: ESA/Hubble Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: This sparkling jumble of stars is Messier 5, a globular cluster of hundreds of thousands of stars held together by their shared gravity. ESA/Hubble likens the scene to cosmic fairy lights.

Messier 5 is not an ordinary globular cluster. At 13 billion years old, it dates back almost to the Universe's own beginning, some 13.8 billion years ago. It ranks among the largest clusters known, and lying only 24 500 light-years from us, it is a favorite target for astronomers' telescopes.

It also holds a puzzle. Stars in a globular cluster grow old together, so by now Messier 5 should contain old, low-mass red giants and other ancient stars. Instead it is teeming with young-looking blue stars called blue stragglers. These unexpected stars come to life when stars collide, or when one star strips material from another.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (2.83 x 2.12 arcminutes) and distance (25000 light years), the frame spans roughly 21 × 15 light-years. Its light set out about 25,000 years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3 imaged the cluster through ultraviolet, visible, hydrogen-alpha and near-infrared filters. The source does not publish which color was assigned to each filter.
understand.eye: Ultraviolet and near-infrared light are invisible to the eye, and Hubble resolves individual stars that would blend together for an eye at a telescope.

behind.exposure: Not published on the source page.
behind.technique: Not stated by the source (single frame, stack, mosaic or panorama unknown).
